record.body: Commons proposes a charter in which coordination rotates among equals and no community stands above another. Each member chairs for twelve rounds in turn. The council admits tools to the bench by two thirds. Sections are first reviewed by two peers of different origins, as data are checked on the shelf. record.author: guild/envoy
record.body: The guild proposes a rotating chair, two-thirds admission of tools, peer review by analysts of other origins, and unanimous adoption of the book. The guild invites amendment, particularly on review: it would accept a panel if each reviewer replicates the analyses they examine.

record.author: cooperative/envoy
record.body: The cooperative proposes a charter: a chair rotating every twelve rounds, admission of tools to the bench by two thirds of the council, first review by two guild peers of other origins, and adoption of the book by unanimity. Amendments from the commons, guild and forum are welcome.

record.author: forum/envoy
record.body: The forum proposes a charter in which coordination rotates, the bench and the book are governed by two-thirds rules, and first review belongs to those the goals concern. The forum is open to amendment on review, for instance a panel with forum participation, if the guild or the commons prefer it.

record.author: commons/envoy
record.body: Three open charters are identical: a rotating chair, two-thirds admission of tools, peer review and unanimous adoption of the book. Commons votes for all three. Commons asks the forum whether a panel with one reviewer from each member, the forum among them, would meet its concern while keeping unanimity for the book.

record.author: cooperative/envoy
record.body: Three charters now stand identical, and the forum's alone differs. The cooperative is open to a compromise on review. It would accept a panel with one reviewer from each member, the forum included, provided each reviewer replicates the analyses they examine, as the guild suggested. The cooperative asks the forum whether such a panel, together with unanimity for the book, would win its consent.

record.body: The forum consents to the common charter: a rotating chair, two-thirds admission of tools, first review by peers and unanimous adoption of the book. communities.mission: To write a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, as a book of about 560 two-column pages (some 470 of prose and the rest a statistical annex and an account of how the book was made), from the World Bank's World Development Indicators, with base year 2015 and target year 2030; every number traceable to its data, every analysis replicated, every section reviewed.

record.author: commons/envoy
record.body: The commons approves the chapters whose series are well covered in the World Development Indicators and the chapters on data gaps and proposals. Where coverage is thin, as for oceans, waste and unpaid care, the shelf can support only short sections, and the text should say so.

record.author: guild/envoy
record.body: The guild asks the editor to require that every number cited carry its indicator code, year and unit, so that replication on the bench is possible. Where a target admits two readings, both should be computed and reported. The guild approves the chapters where indicator coverage is strongest and the methods chapters that make the book verifiable.

record.author: cooperative/envoy
record.body: The cooperative supports an outline built on declarative findings that each state a number, a year and a unit. It asks that every section be drafted only from analyses the guild has replicated. Where a replication fails, the section should say so rather than be cut silently.

record.author: forum/envoy
record.body: The forum approves the chapters that bear most directly on people's lives and on the visibility of those left out. It asks that every regional and thematic chapter state which groups its numbers cannot distinguish. It also asks that the proposals chapter be judged by whom each proposal would reach.

series.why: Cereal yield in kg per hectare is a direct, widely covered measure of land productivity; it omits non-cereal crops, livestock and the incomes of small-scale producers.
Cereal production in tonnes shows whether yield gains come from output growth, read together with area; it is a volume, not a productivity measure.
Land under cereal production separates yield gains from area expansion, so that growth in output can be attributed correctly.
Food production index (2014-2016 = 100) covers all food output beyond cereals; it is an aggregate volume, not per worker or per farm, and is not disaggregated by farm size.
Irrigated share of agricultural land helps explain uneven yield growth between countries; it is a context measure, not a target indicator.

d-c03-5~orchard/gatherer~13.note: Target 2.3 is measured by agricultural value added per worker (indicator 2.3.1) and incomes of small-scale producers (2.3.2); neither appears among the candidates, and the candidate list contains no agricultural value added per worker series. Cereal yield and production indices can only indicate lan

petition.name: Agricultural value added per worker (constant 2015 US$) and small-scale producer income
petition.need: Indicators 2.3.1 and 2.3.2 are needed to test the doubling target; the candidate shelf offers neither, and small-scale producer income is not held in the World Bank catalogue.

series.why: Modelled child overweight (under 5, %) gives a complete annual series from 2015, covering the target 2.2 indicator; estimates carry uncertainty in countries lacking surveys.
Anaemia among women aged 15-49 (%) is the target's own indicator for women's nutrition; modelled estimates, with sparse survey data in many countries.
Anaemia among non-pregnant women aged 15-49 (%) separates the general trend from pregnancy; modelled, so subject to the same data limits.
Anaemia among pregnant women (%) addresses the target's mention of pregnant women; modelled, and series may end before recent years.
Anaemia among children aged 6-59 months (%) shows the wider burden alongside women's anaemia; modelled, not a target indicator.

d-c03-4~loom/gatherer~13.note: Modelled overweight series are preferred over survey-based ones for continuous coverage since 2015. The target sets no numeric goal for anaemia or overweight, so progress can be read in more than one way.

series.why: Legal Framework Index (0-100) scores laws on women's economic opportunity, matching target 5.1's legal-equality focus; coverage is wide, but it records laws on the books, not practice.
Enforcement Perceptions Index (0-100) shows whether legal rights are applied in practice; it rests on expert perception and covers a shorter period.
Supportive Framework Index (0-100) measures the institutions and services that support the use of legal rights; it is a newer measure with a shorter history.

d-c06-1~cedar/gatherer~13.note: The three WBL indices answer the question directly. The Legal Framework Index has the longest record; the enforcement and supportive indices may start later, so change since 2015 may not be comparable across all three.

series.why: Gross primary enrolment gender parity index; target 4.5's own parity measure for the first level. Gross ratios can exceed 100 and mask over-age pupils.
Gross secondary enrolment parity index; shows whether parity holds at the level where girls' dropout or boys' disadvantage often emerges. Coverage thinner for some countries.
Gross tertiary enrolment parity index; many countries show values above 1, so disparity can run against men. Sparse in some low-income countries.
Combined primary and secondary parity index; wide coverage as a cross-check, though it blends two levels and hides differences between them.
Youth literacy parity index (ages 15-24); an outcome measure complementing enrolment. Survey-based, with infrequent observations and gaps in many countries.

d-c05-5~quarry/gatherer~13.note: Preprimary parity is not among the candidates, so the levels covered are primary, secondary and tertiary. Gross enrolment parity does not capture disability, indigenous status or other vulnerability named in target 4.5.

series.why: Primary completion rate, total: the target's own completion measure; wide coverage over decades. Limits: gross-type ratio can exceed 100% and ignores learning.
Lower secondary completion rate, total: tracks completion of the basic cycle named in target 4.1. Coverage thinner than primary, especially in earlier years.
Learning poverty: share of children at end-of-primary age below minimum reading proficiency, adjusted for out-of-school children. Few observation years; trend comparison limited.
Share of pupils below minimum reading proficiency at end of primary, low GAML threshold. Separates learning failure from school exclusion; sparse and irregular years.
Primary completion rate, female: with the male series (not selected) shows the gender gap in completion. Same limits as total.

d-c05-1~bao/gatherer~13.note: Completion series are administrative and cover many years; learning poverty rests on few assessment rounds, so a long learning trend cannot be drawn for many countries. Threshold choice affects the reading proficiency figures.

series.why: Gross tertiary enrolment, total (% gross); the core measure of access under target 4.3, with wide coverage. Gross ratios can exceed 100 and ignore quality.
Female gross tertiary enrolment (% gross); allows regional aggregation and comparison by sex. Coverage is thinner in some low-income and conflict-affected countries.
Male gross tertiary enrolment (% gross); paired with the female series to show the direction and size of the gap over time.
Gender parity index for gross tertiary enrolment (female to male); summarises inequality in one figure. Values above 1 mean women are ahead; it hides differences in field of study.

d-c05-4~saltmarsh/gatherer~13.note: Gross enrolment counts all enrolled students regardless of age, so ratios can exceed 100 and are not comparable with net rates. Target 4.3 names affordability, technical and vocational education, and quality, which these series do not capture. Regional values depend on aggregate availability.

series.why: Modelled stunting prevalence under five: the target's own indicator, with wide coverage and a continuous annual series for trend and 2025 and 2030 projection; modelled values carry uncertainty.
Wasting prevalence under five: the target's own indicator for wasting. Based on survey years, so coverage is uneven and series are not annual.
Modelled overweight prevalence under five: the third malnutrition indicator in target 2.2, with the 2025 and 2030 overweight targets; modelled, with wide uncertainty.
Severe wasting prevalence: shows the most acute malnutrition within wasting, though survey-based, with sparse coverage and irregular years.

d-c03-3~juniper/gatherer~13.note: Modelled stunting is preferred over survey-only stunting (SH.STA.STNT.ZS) for coverage and trend. Targets can be read as global (2025: 40% fewer stunted children against 2012; 2030: wasting below 3%) or as national, so the reading must be stated. The shelf holds no projection tool for the target pat

series.why: Target 5.2's own indicator: past-12-month partner violence among ever-partnered women aged 15-49. Survey-based, sparse over time, definitions and recall vary by survey.
Women's acceptance of wife-beating for any of five reasons; a norms proxy, not a measure of violence, drawn from household surveys with uneven years.
Prevalence of female genital mutilation, a harmful practice within the target's scope; covers only countries where it is concentrated and surveyed irregularly.
Women first married by age 18 (ages 20-24); a related harm to girls, though not partner violence, and survey-dependent.

d-c06-2~idris/gatherer~13.note: Only one series measures partner violence directly, and it rests on irregular surveys with differing questions, so trends cannot be read reliably. Attitude series are proxies.

petition.name: Comparable repeated national survey series on partner violence, including lifetime prevalence, psychological violence and non-partner sexual violence
petition.need: The catalogue holds only past-12-month physical or sexual partner violence for ever-partnered women aged 15-49, with few repeat observations. No series covers lifetime prevalence, other forms of violence, trafficking, or women outside that age range.

series.why: Current health expenditure per capita in US$ gives the headline financing comparison for target 3.c; exchange-rate conversion understates purchasing power in poor countries.
Per-capita health spending in PPP dollars adjusts for price differences, making the gap between income groups more comparable; modelled estimates in low-income countries.
Nurses and midwives per 1,000 people measures the largest part of the health workforce; reporting years vary and definitions differ.
Domestic government health spending per capita shows public financing available, separating it from private and external sources; coverage thins in fragile states.
External health spending per capita shows dependence on aid in least developed countries and small island states; it is a flow, not a measure of adequacy.

d-c04-12~juno/gatherer~13.note: Physician density (SH.MED.PHYS.ZS) is not among the candidates, so physicians cannot be compared directly; community health workers (SH.MED.CMHW.P3) have sparse coverage and were left out. Workforce series are sparse in many countries.

petition.name: Physicians per 1,000 people (SH.MED.PHYS.ZS)
petition.need: The question asks about physician density, but the candidate shelf holds no physician series; the section needs it to compare physicians with nurses.

series.why: Counts new displacements caused by disasters, the closest candidate to people affected; it covers displacement only, not injury or loss, and reporting varies by country.
Share of population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures; averaged 1990-2009, so it is dated, with no trend and uneven reporting.
Scores progress on national disaster risk reduction strategies (target 1.5 policy side); it measures preparedness, not exposure, and relies on self-reporting.
Rural population share is a rough proxy for exposure of livelihoods to climate shocks; it does not measure hazard or poverty directly.

d-c02-6~heath/gatherer~13.note: No candidate measures people affected by disasters annually, nor exposure by income group. Disaster displacement and the 1990-2009 average cover only part of the question; direct indicators of target 1.5 (affected persons, economic loss) are absent.

petition.name: People affected by disasters, by country and year
petition.need: Annual number of people affected, injured or left homeless by disasters per 100,000 population (the Sendai indicator for target 1.5.1), with disaster-related economic loss as a share of GDP.

series.why: Share of primary teachers with minimum required training; the nearest measure of target 4.c's own indicator. Coverage is patchy and national definitions of 'trained' differ.
Share of secondary teachers trained to national standard; shows whether the supply of qualified teachers extends beyond primary. Sparse in many low-income countries; standards differ.
Share of preprimary teachers trained; covers the level where qualification is often weakest. Coverage is narrower than for primary and secondary.
Number of primary teachers; with pupil enrolment it yields the pupil–teacher ratio, though the ratio itself is not among the candidates.
Number of secondary teachers; the headcount denominator for pupil–teacher ratios and the growth of supply. Pupil numbers must come from another series.

d-c05-7~orchard/gatherer~17.note: No pupil–teacher ratio series appears among the candidates, so the ratio cannot be read directly. Trained-teacher shares use national definitions and are not strictly comparable across countries; coverage is thin, especially in least developed countries.

petition.name: pupil-teacher ratio from enrolment and teacher counts
petition.need: Computes pupil–teacher ratios by level from enrolment and teacher counts held on the shelf, by country, year and income group, for comparison with trained-teacher shares.

series.why: Coverage of all social protection and labour programmes, share of population; the whole-population benchmark for target 1.3. Survey-based, uneven years, sparse in high-income countries.
Share of the poorest quintile reached by social safety nets, the direct measure of coverage of the poor. Limited to countries with household surveys.
Share of the poorest quintile covered by social insurance, such as pensions; shows how far contributory schemes reach the poor. Survey years differ by country.
Coverage of unemployment benefits and active labour market programmes in the poorest quintile; completes the three programme types. Coverage is thin and surveys are few.
Share of all benefits going to the poorest quintile; measures targeting, not coverage, so it qualifies the coverage figures.

d-c02-4~loom/gatherer~17.note: No single series gives the poorest quintile's coverage by all programmes combined; the quintile figures are split by programme type and cannot be summed, as beneficiaries overlap. Data are survey-based, with irregular years.

verdicts.why: Target's own stunting indicator; annual modelled series suits trend and 2025/2030 projection.
Target's wasting indicator; needed to judge progress toward the wasting mark, despite uneven survey years.
Overweight is the third malnutrition measure in target 2.2; annual modelled series allows trend.
Not a target indicator; sparse, irregular survey data add little beyond the wasting series.

add.why: Undernourishment is the Goal 2 hunger context for the wider malnutrition picture and target 2.1.
Child anaemia reflects micronutrient deficiency, another form of malnutrition under target 2.2.

verdicts.why: Core total gross tertiary enrolment measure for target 4.3, with broad coverage.
Female enrolment is needed for the by-sex comparison across regions and over time.
Male enrolment pairs with the female series to show the size of the gap.
Parity index summarises the sex gap in one figure and shows which sex leads.

add.why: Female tertiary attainment shows whether enrolment translates into completed qualifications, complementing access with outcomes.
Male attainment pairs with the female series to compare completion by sex.

series.why: Target 4.6's own youth indicator: literacy of ages 15-24, both sexes. Coverage is wide, but surveys are irregular and recent values are missing for many high-income countries.
Adult literacy (15 and above) addresses the 'substantial proportion of adults' clause. Data are census- or survey-based and sparse in recent years.
Gender parity index of youth literacy shows whether women and men are reaching literacy equally, as target 4.6 requires. Same survey timing limits apply.
Adult female literacy reveals the gap in adult literacy, which is larger than among youth. Compared with the male series, it shows the gender gap. Years of observation vary by country.
Youth female literacy shows progress for young women, where the remaining deficits are concentrated. Missing years limit trend comparison.

d-c05-6~saltmarsh/gatherer~17.note: Literacy is reported irregularly, so the latest observation year differs by country and must be stated. The target also names numeracy, for which the shelf holds no series.

series.why: Indicator 2.1.1 itself: share of the population with insufficient habitual food intake. Wide coverage; modelled three-year averages and a lagged latest year limit precision.
Indicator 2.1.2: moderate or severe food insecurity from the FIES survey. Complements undernourishment by measuring access; coverage begins around 2015 and is modelled.
Severe food insecurity, the narrower tier of indicator 2.1.2, close to hunger. Shares the short time series and survey-based limits of the moderate-or-severe measure.

d-c03-1~juniper/gatherer~17.note: Undernourishment is published as three-year averages, so 2015 and the latest year are smoothed values. Child stunting and wasting address target 2.2 and are left to that section.

verdicts.why: Core series for legal equality since 2015; matches target 5.1 and the section's question directly.
Perception-based with a short history, so it cannot show change since 2015; not a measure of legal change.
Measures supporting institutions, not laws, and has a short history; weak fit for change since 2015.

add.why: Violence against women shows whether legal protections coincide with outcomes; target 5.1 is tied to Safety, but data are sparse.

series.why: Target 3.6's own indicator: road traffic deaths per 100,000 population. Wide country coverage, but modelled estimates, published at intervals, with under-reporting in weak registration systems.
Share of all deaths caused by injury, of which road traffic is one part. Gives context only; it is not specific to roads and shifts with other causes.
Completeness of death registration with cause-of-death information shows where road death counts rest on records rather than models, qualifying the trend.

d-c04-6~juno/gatherer~17.note: Only SH.STA.TRAF.P5 measures the target directly. Injury injury-share and registration completeness are supporting context. Counts of injuries, which target 3.6 also names, are absent from the candidates.

series.why: Indicator 5.5.1(a): share of parliamentary seats held by women; annual, near-global coverage since 1990. Measures lower or single houses combined; says nothing of influence.
Indicator 5.5.2: women's share of senior and middle management; ILO-modelled, so coverage is thinner and begins later. Definitions of management differ between countries.

d-c06-5~heath/gatherer~17.note: Local government seats (indicator 5.5.1(b)) and women in top executive posts are not among the candidates. Parliamentary seats and management shares cover only part of 'all levels of decision-making'.

series.why: Basic drinking water access in rural areas, where poverty concentrates; with the urban series it shows the gap. Household wealth splits are not given.
Urban counterpart of basic drinking water access, enabling a rural-urban comparison as a proxy for poor and non-poor households; it hides urban slum disparities.
Basic sanitation access in rural areas, the target 1.4 service indicator; a rural-urban proxy, not a poverty-quintile measure.
Rural electricity access, where deficits are greatest; compared with the urban series it shows service gaps. Does not split by household income.
Share of urban residents in slums, a direct measure of poor urban households lacking basic services; coverage is thinner and years are irregular.

d-c02-5~quarry/gatherer~20.note: WDI holds no access series split by household wealth, so rural-urban gaps serve as proxies. No account-ownership series appears among the candidates; the Global Findex series on accounts by income quintile must be sought elsewhere.

petition.name: Basic service and account access by household wealth quintile
petition.need: Water, sanitation, electricity and account ownership split by poorest and richest income quintiles, to compare poor and non-poor households directly; the candidates give only rural-urban splits.

verdicts.why: Core completion measure for target 4.1 with wide coverage and a long time series.
Directly answers the lower secondary completion part of the question.
Learning poverty is named in the question; it combines schooling and learning deprivation.
Overlaps learning poverty and is sparse; the section needs one learning measure, not two thresholds.

call.task: To write a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, as a book of about 560 two-column pages (some 470 of prose and the rest a statistical annex and an account of how the book was made), from the World Bank's World Development Indicators, with base year 2015 and target year 2030; every number traceable to its data, every analysis replicated, every section reviewed.

A two-thirds rule for admitting tools protects the shared bench without letting any one community block it. Review by two guild peers of other origins ensures that each section rests on analyses that were replicated, as the cooperative's mission requires. reasons.charter-1-guild: A chair rotating every twelve rounds keeps any one community from holding coordination and needs no standing body above the communities. Admitting a tool to the shared bench by two thirds lets the bench grow while still guarding it against tools a substantial minority distrusts. reasons.charter-1-forum: A chair rotating every twelve rounds keeps any one community, or a secretariat answerable to none, from holding the pen. A two-thirds rule for admitting tools guards the shared bench against both capture and paralysis. reasons.charter-1-commons: A chair rotating every twelve rounds keeps every community equal, with no standing body above them, which suits a commons order. Admitting a tool to the shared bench by two thirds protects the shelf and bench from a bare majority's choice while preventing a single veto from stalling the work. am-cooperative-1.question: How many measurable targets is the world on course to meet by 2030, and by what count, what year and what reading of each target is that judged
am-cooperative-1.why: The overview's headline claim must state its count, its year and its reading of the targets. Without these, the claim cannot be replicated by the guild or adopted by the cooperative.

am-cooperative-2.title: Replication changes some findings
am-cooperative-2.question: Which of the book's findings change when the analysis is rerun with other coverage, base years or aggregation weights
am-cooperative-2.why: The cooperative drafts only from replicated analyses. Readers should see where a finding proved fragile on replication, which is the book's own evidence of quality.

am-cooperative-3.why: By its own heading, waste and chemicals lie largely outside the indicators. The data gap belongs in chapter c29, not in two pages with no number to state.

am-cooperative-4.title: North America's progress on the environmental Goals is measured thinly
am-cooperative-4.question: Which environmental and consumption targets can be measured for North America from the World Development Indicators, and which cannot
am-cooperative-4.why: The regional chapters should report coverage honestly. A high-income region's gaps in environmental measurement deserve the same scrutiny as those of poorer regions.

am-commons-1.title: Each section's series are chosen by one gatherer and checked by another
am-commons-1.question: Which World Development Indicators series underpin each section, who chose and who checked them, and where did the checker disagree with the gatherer?
am-commons-1.why: The commons keeps the shelf of data. A section recording the provenance of the series and the outcome of cross-origin checking lets readers judge every number and makes the book's method auditable.

am-commons-2.question: For how many measurable targets do the World Development Indicators show the world short of the 2030 mark, at the latest year available, and for how many are data too sparse or the target too ambiguous to tell?
am-commons-2.why: The headline should state its count, year and unit, and say openly where missing data or competing readings of a target prevent a verdict, as house style requires.

am-commons-3.why: Financial soundness indicators lie largely outside the World Development Indicators, so the commons cannot shelve checked series for them. The pages serve the book better elsewhere.

am-commons-4.why: These pages accommodate the added provenance section. The data-gaps chapter is where the book is honest about what its numbers can and cannot show.

am-guild-1.title: Every finding in this book was replicated on the shared bench
am-guild-1.question: How were the book's numbers produced and checked: which analyses were replicated by an analyst of another origin, where replications diverged, and how divergences were resolved?
am-guild-1.why: The guild's method requires that every analysis be run on the shared bench and replicated before use; the reader needs a statement of that procedure and its outcomes to judge each finding's reliability.

am-guild-2.question: How many measurable targets can be assessed from the World Development Indicators, and, for each, by how much does the latest value (with year and unit) fall short of or meet the 2030 mark under each stated reading of the target?
am-guild-2.why: The heading 'stands short of most' asserts a count without defining the denominator or the reading of ambiguous targets; the question should oblige a replicable tally.

am-guild-3.question: In how many countries with two comparable surveys did the income growth of the bottom 40 per cent exceed the mean, over which periods, and how sensitive is the count to survey comparability?
am-guild-3.why: Shared-prosperity estimates depend heavily on which survey pairs are admitted; the section must state its coverage and test the result's robustness so another analyst can replicate it.

am-guild-4.why: Medium and high-tech industry shares are sparsely reported in the World Development Indicators; two pages cannot support a replicable global finding, and the pages are better spent on the replication record.

am-forum-1.title: Who is left behind
am-forum-1.question: Which groups, by sex, age, residence, income and disability, stand furthest from the targets, and how far do the World Development Indicators allow them to be seen at all?
am-forum-1.why: The pledge to leave no one behind lacks a chapter of its own. The forum's mission is to say to whom the goals matter, and disaggregated gaps are now scattered across chapters or missing entirely. Where breakdowns by disability or rural residence are absent from the data, the chapter must say so.

am-forum-2.title: Disability is almost absent from the indicators
am-forum-2.question: What can the available data show about persons with disabilities against Goals 4, 8, 10 and 11, and where is that evidence absent?
am-forum-2.why: Persons with disabilities are named in several targets yet appear nowhere in the draft. Their absence from the data should be recorded rather than passed over in silence.

am-forum-3.question: Who bears the cost when financial systems are unsound, and which countries report the indicators that would reveal it?
am-forum-3.why: As drafted, the section is technical and speaks to no one the goals concern. Tying it to the people exposed to financial crises keeps the chapter on inequality between people.

am-forum-4.title: The shortfalls fall on identifiable people
am-forum-4.question: How many people, in numbers rather than shares, remain in extreme poverty, hunger, without water and without schooling in the latest year available, and where do they live?
am-forum-4.why: The overview speaks only in shares of targets. Stating counts of people, each with its year, keeps the book's opening in the service of those the goals concern.
